analysis.one_liner: Created a government-run Medicare drug plan that would negotiate prices directly with drug manufacturers.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced in October 2007 with 9 cosponsors, never left the Senate Finance Committee and died when the Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required Medicare to offer its own prescription drug plan nationwide starting in 2009, alongside the private plans seniors choose from today. Medicare would have negotiated drug prices directly with manufacturers, using the same kinds of strategies as other big federal buyers like the VA, and charged one uniform national premium based on actual cost. It also set up an appeals process for denied claims and required the plan to pay pharmacies promptly.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries, especially the roughly 25 million seniors and disabled people who lacked drug coverage before Part D, would have gained a government-run plan option with nationally uniform premiums and prices negotiated directly with drug makers — a public alternative to the private insurance middlemen who run Part D plans today. Community pharmacies would also have gained a guarantee of prompt payment (14 days for electronic claims, 30 for paper).

how_it_helps.text: Starting in 2009, the Secretary of Health and Human Services would have had to offer one or more Medicare-operated drug plans with a service area covering the entire United States, giving beneficiaries a public option alongside private Part D plans.

For that plan, the Secretary would have been required to negotiate purchase prices directly with pharmaceutical manufacturers and encourage use of more affordable therapeutic equivalents, using strategies similar to those of other federal purchasers such as the VA — authority private Part D plans do not have.

The public plan's monthly premium would have been uniform nationally and based on the average per-person cost of running the plan, including administrative expenses, rather than set market-by-market by private insurers.

Beneficiaries denied a drug under the plan would have gotten a defined appeals process, including review by an independent outside entity, designed to be quick and low-hassle when a drug is medically necessary.
Pharmacies filling prescriptions under the public plan would have been paid for clean claims within 14 days (electronic) or 30 days (paper), with unpaid claims deemed approved and paid.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers would have borne the main cost, in the form of lower negotiated prices and pressure to substitute cheaper therapeutically equivalent drugs. Private Part D insurers would have lost enrollment and pricing power to a competing public plan. Because the plan's premium was designed to cover its own average cost, taxpayers would not have directly subsidized enrollees' premiums beyond standard Part D subsidies.
analysis.who_pays_short: Brand-name drug makers and private drug plans

drawbacks.text: The public plan's formulary tools included prior authorization, step therapy, and reference pricing, and it was required to steer patients toward cheaper drugs with similar clinical benefit — meaning some beneficiaries might not get quick access to the specific drug their doctor first prescribed.

Negotiated prices and required use of therapeutic equivalents would cut directly into brand-name drug companies' revenue, and the industry's long-standing objection to government price negotiation is that lower revenue could mean less investment in developing new medicines — the trade-off any price-negotiation scheme carries.

The bill would have replaced the existing 'fallback' drug plans (a thin public backstop under the 2003 law) with the new Medicare-operated plan rather than simply adding to the private market, a restructuring that private plans and pharmacies would have had to adapt to.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For beneficiaries, the upside was concrete: a public drug plan whose premiums covered actual cost and whose prices were negotiated the way the VA negotiates, plus a real appeals process and prompt pharmacy payment. The costs fell mostly on drug makers and private insurers rather than on enrollees, though the trade-off was a tighter formulary — cheaper therapeutic equivalents first, with prior authorization and appeals standing between some patients and the exact drug first prescribed. On balance the design aimed savings at beneficiaries and costs at the industries that profit from Part D's current structure.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and the committee never took it up — no hearing, no markup, no vote — before the Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Sen. Dick Durbin introduced the bill on October 23, 2007, for himself and Senators Akaka, Stabenow, Boxer, and Obama, and it drew 9 cosponsors (8 Democrats and 1 Independent).
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance, the committee with jurisdiction over Medicare.
That referral was the last action ever taken: the action history shows no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action, through the end of the 110th Congress on January 3, 2009.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private Part D insurers and brand-name drug manufacturers came out ahead: Medicare's drug benefit continued to run exclusively through private plans with no government-negotiated prices and no public plan competitor, exactly the arrangement the bill would have changed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private drug plans and brand-name drug makers

for.name: Dick Durbin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on October 23, 2007 and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

for.name: Barack Obama
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original cosponsor when the bill was introduced.

for.name: Daniel Akaka, Barbara Boxer, and Debbie Stabenow
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors, alongside 5 additional senators who signed on later, bringing total cosponsorship to 9.

against.name: Max Baucus
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on October 23, 2007 and never scheduled a markup or vote on the bill for the remaining 14 months of the Congress.

against.name: Pharmaceutical industry (PhRMA)
against.what_they_did: Opposed letting the government negotiate Medicare drug prices, a position it maintained against every version of the proposal during this period.

against.name: Private Medicare drug plan insurers
against.what_they_did: Resisted a government-run plan option that would compete directly with their Part D plans, which were created under the 2003 Medicare law as the exclusive way to receive the drug benefit.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so no roll-call positions exist; all 10 Senate supporters — Durbin and his 9 cosponsors — were Democrats or the chamber's Independent.

industries.note: The bill would have required Medicare to negotiate purchase prices directly and to steer patients to cheaper therapeutic equivalents, cutting into the prices and sales volume that brand-name drugs command under Part D. Under current law the government is barred from negotiating, so manufacturers keep private-plan negotiated prices high.

A nationally available Medicare-operated plan would have competed head-to-head with the private insurers that administer every Part D plan today, and the bill would have eliminated the existing fallback plans after 2008. Insurers profit from administrating the drug benefit without any public competitor.

The bill guaranteed pharmacies payment for clean claims within 14 days (electronic) or 30 days (paper), with slow-walked claims deemed payable — addressing a chronic cash-flow complaint under private plan payment systems.
